title: Ground-up green industrialization: learning from, leveraging and scaling Africa’s neglected ecosystem
body:
When we think of green industrialization in Africa, we often jump straight to high-tech industries. While this is good, the framing creates two problems: it fuels the false narrative that Africa lacks a foundation for green industrialization and blinds us to opportunities hiding in plain sight.

Africa’s repair, scrap, and recycling ecosystems represent one of such opportunities. They are already performing essential circular economy functions including, recovering value, extending product lifecycles and reducing waste. But even more importantly, they generate knowledge.

Inside these ecosystems, workers and micro-enterprises continuously learn by doing. They experiment, adapt, and refine techniques with little or no policy support, infrastructure, or formal recognition.

Yet these ecosystems are rarely recognized as part of industrial policy. This is a major industrial policy blind spot.

Africa’s green industrialization, especially as it concerns circular economy will not emerge only from high-tech plants and imported solutions.

It will also be built from what already exists. This includes the repair workshop, scrap yard, e-waste cluster and ultimately, the millions of workers who are already learning, adapting, and innovating every day.

**Implication:** Africa’s industrialization challenge isn't necessary a lack of foundation. It is not fully recognizing or leveraging the one it already has.

This is evident as, too often, policy approaches across the continent aim to formalize or replace informal systems, assuming that progress requires starting over. This limits Africa’s window of opportunity and risks destroying accumulated knowledge instead of building on it.

A more strategic approach requires that these ecosystems become the entry point for Africa’s green industrialization, bridging low-tech recovery activities with higher-value recycling, manufacturing, and green production. Given that they also hold immense “LEARNING” opportunities, amid limited policy support and resource constraints, they are industrial learning platform. This isn't trivial given Africa’s fragmented learning system in the formal sector.

From an industrial policy perspective, African policymakers must therefore:

- Learn from this ecosystem on how innovation, skills, and circularity emerge organically under resource constraint and outside formal institutions
- Leverage this ecosystem as hubs for green skills and entry points into circular value chains
- Scale this ecosystem through upgrading, integration into formal industrial systems, and enabling growth from micro to small, and from small to industrial scale

**Bottom Line:** Africa’s repair, scrap and recycle ecosystems are not peripheral. They are a ground-up industrial learning platform.

The task is thus clear: Learn from it. Leverage it. Scale it.
